questions.question: In Notice writing, the name of the institution/organisation is placed
questions.answer:
**(C)** at the top

A notice is issued in the name of an institution, so the **name of the school, college or organisation is written at the very top**, above the word "NOTICE" and the date. A reader must know at once on whose authority the announcement is made.

questions.question: In a letter to Editor salutation is written just after
questions.answer:
**(C)** Subject

The order in a formal letter is: sender's address and date → receiver's address → **subject line** → salutation ("Sir/Madam") → body. The salutation therefore comes immediately **after the subject**, which tells the reader what the letter is about before the greeting.

questions.question: What is the correct way to write the subscription in a formal letter?
options: your truly (both words in lower case)
Yours truly (only the first word capitalised)
questions.answer:
**(C)** Yours truly

The subscription of a formal letter is written as "**Yours truly**" — only the first word is capitalised, and the second word is in lower case. "Yours Truly" capitalises both words and is wrong; "your truly" and "your Truly" are both misspelt and wrongly capitalised.

questions.question: In report writing, the language used should be
questions.answer:
**(D)** Ambiguous — *none of the four is right*

The options as printed are all negative or irrelevant: a report is written in **clear, simple, objective and formal** language. Of the four, "Ambiguous" is the only one that even describes a quality of language, and it is the one a report must **avoid**; the other three ("loud", "whispering") describe the volume of speech, not written language.

**How to answer in the exam.** The intended answer is **(D)**, chosen by elimination: a report cannot be loud, unclear or whispering in the literal sense, and the examiner's point is that its style must be plain and unambiguous. Write "(D) Ambiguous — because a report must be clear, not ambiguous", as the paper's own options are faulty here.

questions.question: Name of the poem of the given lines is: 'I saw my mother, beside me, doze, open mouthed, her face ashen like that of a corpse and realised with pain that she was as old as she looked but soon put that thought away, and looked out at Young trees sprinting, the merry children spilling out of their homes.'
options: Elementary School Classroom in a Slum
questions.answer:
**(B)** My Mother at Sixty-six

The lines are from **My Mother at Sixty-Six** by Kamala Das. The poet sits beside her dozing mother in a car on the way to Cochin airport, sees her face "ashen like that of a corpse", and then looks out at "young trees sprinting" and "merry children spilling out of their homes" to escape the thought of death.

questions.question: The poet's mother is described as 'open-mouthed' because
questions.answer:
**(D)** She was dozing

The line reads "doze, open mouthed". Her mouth has fallen open because she is **asleep** — an old woman dozing in a moving car — and it is this unguarded, slack face that makes the daughter see her as "ashen like that of a corpse".

questions.question: In the given extract the phrase 'realised with pain' indicates the poet's
questions.answer:
**(A)** anxiety

"Realised with pain that she was as old as she looked" expresses the poet's **anxiety** — her fear of losing her mother, and through it the fear of her own ageing and death. It is the "old familiar ache" of her childhood returning, not a memory of the past, a state of despair or any illness of her own.

questions.question: According to the poet, the thing of beauty is
questions.answer:
**(B)** A joy forever

Keats opens the poem with exactly this line — "**A thing of beauty is a joy for ever**". Its loveliness "increases", "it will never pass into nothingness", and it keeps "a bower quiet for us, and a sleep / Full of sweet dreams and health, and quiet breathing".

questions.question: The story 'The Last Lesson' highlights which human tendency?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Procrastination

The story turns on the habit of putting off what should be done today. Franz has not learnt his participles — "I had counted on the commotion... to get to my desk without being seen" — and the village people regret not having sent their children to school while they could. M. Hamel blames himself and the parents for postponing learning, and the order from Berlin makes the postponement permanent: "we've always thought there would be time".

questions.question: Who is Mr. Lamb?
questions.answer:
**(B)** An old man

Mr. Lamb is an **old man** who lives alone in a house with a large garden and a tin leg lost in the war. Derry, a boy of fourteen, climbs over the wall and finds him there; the play is the conversation between the old man and the boy about looks, fear and acceptance.

questions.chapter: Journey to the End of the Earth
questions.question: Who gives us an insight into the world's geological history?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Study of Antarctica Continent

Tishani Doshi writes that the **study of the Antarctica continent** — its ice cores, its rocks and its fossils — gives us an insight into the world's geological history. The continent holds the record of Gondwana's break-up, of the dinosaurs and of the climate of half a billion years, which is why scientists call its ice "the earth's memory".

questions.question: Who is the author of 'Indigo'?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Louis Fischer

"Indigo" is a chapter from **Louis Fischer's** book *The Life of Mahatma Gandhi*. It describes the Champaran campaign of 1917 — the sharecroppers bound to grow indigo, the British landlords, and the movement that became the first victory of civil disobedience in India.

questions.question: What did Roger's mother decide finally?
options: To take him back to awful wizard and get his smell back
questions.answer:
**(A)** To take him back to awful wizard and get his smell back

In "Should Wizard Hit Mommy?" Roger Skunk's mother is angry that the wizard has made her son smell of roses: "he is a skunk and he must smell like a skunk". She **takes him back to the awful wizard and gets his own smell back** — and refuses to let the wizard change him again.

*(This chapter is outside the current syllabus but the question appears in this paper.)*

questions.question: What was the name of the school where Zitkala-Sa studied?
questions.answer:
**(A)** Carlisle Indian School

Zitkala-Sa was sent to the **Carlisle Indian School** in Pennsylvania, a boarding school run on the principle of "civilising" Native American children. There her long hair was cut off, an experience she records in "The Cutting of My Long Hair" as the loss of her identity.

questions.question: Why do the celebrities feel embarrassed most often?
options: Because of question attack during interviews
questions.answer:
**(A)** Because of question attack during interviews

Celebrities feel embarrassed because an interview becomes an **attack of questions** — some of them personal, some hostile, and all of them printed as if they were the person's settled opinion. The chapter quotes writers who call the interview an intrusion, "an affront", even "immoral", precisely because the person being interviewed is at the mercy of the questions.

questions.question: The rag pickers have no identity but they have
questions.answer:
**(C)** Ration cards

In "Lost Spring" the ragpickers of Seemapuri live "without an identity and without permits", but they **do have ration cards** that enable them to vote and buy grain. As Anees Jung puts it, "food is more important for them than their identity".

questions.question: Whenever terror struck again, Douglas would start
questions.answer:
**(D)** Talking to terror

In "Deep Water" Douglas writes that whenever the old terror returned, he would **talk to it**: he would say aloud, "Well, Mr Terror, what do you think you can do to me?" and swim on. The device worked because it turned a blind fear into something he could face and answer.

questions.question: Where do their lives 'slyly turn'?
questions.answer:
**(A)** In their cramped holes

In "An Elementary School Classroom in a Slum" Spender writes of the slum children that "their lives, that slyly turn in their cramped holes / From fog to endless night". Their whole existence is confined to **cramped holes** — their narrow, dark dwellings — with no view of the sun or of the world the classroom map promises.

*(This chapter is outside the current syllabus but the question appears in this paper.)*

questions.question: 'Clear rills' are the
questions.answer:
**(B)** Streams of clear water

A "rill" is a small stream, so the "clear rills" of Keats's poem are **streams of clear water** that "make for themselves a cooling covert against the hot season". They are one of the natural beauties that give man "a sleep full of sweet dreams, and health, and quiet breathing".

questions.question: 'Full of sweet dreams' means
questions.answer:
**(A)** Pleasant and peaceful sleep

The phrase comes from "a sleep / Full of sweet dreams and health, and quiet breathing" and means a **pleasant and peaceful sleep** — the rest that beautiful things give to a tired mind. It is the opposite of the disturbed sleep and nightmares in the other options.

questions.question: 'Denizens' of a world of green means
questions.answer:
**(A)** residents of forests

A "denizen" is an inhabitant or resident. The tigers are "bright topaz denizens of a world of green" — the yellow beasts who **live in the green forest** of Aunt Jennifer's embroidered panel. The word gives the tigers a home and a belonging that their maker does not have.

questions.question: Who wanted to feel the money at hand and from whom?
options: The rural folk from the government
The rural folk from the social agencies
The rural folk from government officials
The rural folk from city people
questions.answer:
**(D)** The rural folk from city people

In "A Roadside Stand" the villagers say: "Here far from the city we make our roadside stand / And ask for some **city money** to feel in hand". The **rural folk** want to feel the money they earn from the **city people** who pass in their cars — not a grant from the government or an agency.

questions.question: According to the poet wars that are fought have no
questions.answer:
**(D)** Survivors

In "Keeping Quiet" Neruda writes of "those who prepare green wars, / wars with gas, wars with fire, / victory with no survivors". A modern war leaves **no survivors** — the poet's warning against the weapons that make victory indistinguishable from total destruction.

questions.question: How does Umberto Eco find so much time to write so much?
options: Using free times like waiting for someone, break time etc.
questions.answer:
**(D)** Using free times like waiting for someone, break time etc.

Umberto Eco says that he **works in the interstices of time** — while waiting for someone, in a lift, during a break, on a train. He explains that his novels were written "in the cracks" of a busy academic life, which is why he can produce so much: he uses **free time** rather than finding a large block of it.

questions.question: Why does Derry begin to weep in the end?
options: Out of relief as had managed to come
Mr. Lamb did not want him
His mother prohibited him from stepping
questions.answer:
**(A)** Out of relief as he had managed to come

Derry **weeps out of relief** — he has overcome his fear and his shame and has come back to the garden, and in doing so has chosen life over the isolation his burnt face had imposed on him. The weeping is the release of a boy who has at last been listened to and believed in.

**Note on the play's ending.** He arrives to find that Mr. Lamb has fallen from the ladder and died, which makes the moment both a relief and a grief: he has lost the one person who understood him, but he has become the person Mr. Lamb wanted him to be.

questions.question: Bama's brother was asked by the landlord's men
questions.answer:
**(D)** his caste

In "We Too Are Human Beings" Bama's elder brother tells her that the landlord's men asked him **his caste** when he went to deliver a message — and when he answered, they made him wait outside and would not let him touch the parcel. The question of caste, asked at the door, is the whole system of untouchability in one sentence.

questions.question: How old was the Prince when he ridiculed the astrologer?
questions.answer:
**(A)** 10 days

In "The Tiger King" the ten-day-old prince — still an infant — **speaks and ridicules the astrologer**, asking him how he could possibly know the manner of his death when "all those who are born will one day have to die". The astrologer then names the tiger, and the whole campaign begins from that cradle.

questions.question: Who has written the poem 'Keeping Quiet'?
questions.answer:
**(A)** Pablo Neruda

**Keeping Quiet** is by the Chilean poet **Pablo Neruda**. The other three wrote "A Thing of Beauty" (Keats), "The Thought-Fox" (Hughes) and "Aunt Jennifer's Tigers" (Rich).

questions.question: Why did Hamel blame himself?
options: Not having taught them enough French
questions.answer:
**(A)** Not having taught them enough French

M. Hamel blames himself for **not having taught the children enough French** — for having sent them to water his flowers, for giving them a holiday when he wanted to go fishing, and for letting them treat the language carelessly. "It is the great trouble with Alsace," he says, "that it puts off learning till tomorrow" — and he includes himself among those who put it off.

questions.question: What forces children to live a life of exploitation?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Poverty

In "Lost Spring" **poverty** forces children into a life of exploitation: Saheb scrounges in the garbage because his family has nothing, and the bangle-makers of Firozabad put their children at the furnaces because the family cannot survive without those extra hands. Anees Jung's point is that the children have no choice — they are born into a trade and a debt they cannot escape.

questions.question:
Read the passage from Bacon's essay 'Of Studies' and answer any six of the following:
(a) What is the main purpose of study?
(b) What is the main use of study as an ornament?
(c) What marks the humour of a scholar?
(d) What can expert men do about studies?
(e) Write similar words from the passage for (i) Happiness (ii) Rest.
(f) What is the passage all about?
(g) Studies are contemned by whom?
(h) Write the antonym of 'notice' from the passage.
questions.answer:
### (a)

**Answer.** The main purpose of study is **threefold — delight, ornament and ability**: "their chief use for delight is in privateness and retiring; for ornament, is in discourse; and for ability, is in the judgement and disposition of business".

**The passage's own words.**

> "STUDIES serve for delight, for ornament, and for ability."

**In one line.** Study gives private pleasure in solitude, adds grace to conversation and sharpens a man's judgement in the conduct of business.

### (b)

**Answer.** The main use of study as an **ornament** is **in discourse** — that is, in conversation and in speech. Learning gives a man the ability to talk well and to adorn his conversation with knowledge.

**The passage's own words.**

> "for ornament, is in discourse"

**Explained.** Bacon's three uses are private and public: *delight* in "privateness and retiring", *ornament* in "discourse", and *ability* in "the judgement and disposition of business". A learned man's talk is his ornament — but the passage warns that to use learning only for ornament is "affectation".

### (c)

**Answer.** To **make judgement wholly by their rules** is the humour of a scholar — that is, the scholar's eccentricity is to judge the affairs of the world entirely by the rules learnt from books.

**The passage's own words.**

> "to make judgement wholly by their rules is the humour of a scholar"

**Explained.** "Humour" here means a peculiar trait or temperament. Bacon's charge is that bookish men try to fit life to theory: their learning is real, but they lack the flexibility of "expert men" who can "execute, and perhaps judge of particulars, one by one".

### (d)

**Answer.** **Expert men can execute, and perhaps judge of particulars, one by one**; but the general counsels, and the plots and marshalling of affairs, come best from those who are learned.

**The passage's own words.**

> "for expert men can execute, and perhaps judge of particulars, one by one; but the general counsels, and the plots and marshalling of affairs come best from those that are learned."

**Explained.** The expert and the learned are complementary: the practical man handles the individual case, while the trained mind plans the whole campaign. Studies alone will not make a man able; it is "a wisdom without them and above them, won by observation".

### (e)

**Answer.** (a) Happiness — **delight**; (b) Rest — **retiring** (the passage's phrase "privateness and retiring" means withdrawal and repose).

**As used in the passage.**

> "STUDIES serve for **delight**, for ornament, and for ability. Their chief use for delight is in privateness and **retiring**..."

**Note.** "Delight" is exact for happiness. For "rest" the closest word the passage uses is "retiring" — retirement from company into privacy — which is the sense in which it is offered here.

### (f)

**Answer.** The passage is about **the uses and the abuses of study** — why we read, what study does for a man, and how learning can be spoilt by being misused.

**The argument in three steps.** First, studies serve "for delight, for ornament, and for ability". Second, they corrupt their own use if misused: "to spend too much time in studies is sloth; to use them too much for ornament is affectation; to make judgement wholly by their rules is the humour of a scholar". Third, they "perfect nature, and are perfected by experience" — and the wisdom that uses them best is "won by observation". It is Bacon's essay *Of Studies* in miniature.

### (g)

**Answer.** Studies are **contemned by crafty men** — "crafty men contemn studies, simple men admire them, and wise men use them".

**The passage's own words.**

> "Crafty men contemn studies, simple men admire them, and wise men use them."

**Explained.** Bacon gives three attitudes: the **crafty** (the cunning, the worldly-wise) despise book learning because they believe they can manage by their wits; the **simple** are overawed by it; only the **wise** make practical use of it. The sentence is a warning against both contempt and worship.

### (h)

**Answer.** **Contemn** (as in "crafty men **contemn** studies").

**Why this is the answer.** "To notice" is to pay attention to, to value, to regard. "Contemn" means to treat with contempt — to look down on and disregard — so it is the passage's own word of opposite meaning. The paper's key word is the verb "contemn" (the modern form is "condemn/despise").

questions.question: Who was the Crofter? Why did he welcome the peddler so heartily? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The crofter was an **old man who had once worked on the Ramsjö ironworks estate** and now lived alone in a little cottage by the roadside. His sons had left him and his wife was dead, so he kept a cow and sold its milk to the creamery.

He welcomed the peddler **heartily because he was lonely**. On a dark night, when the peddler knocked, the old man "was pleased to get someone to talk to" — he gave him supper, porridge and a bed, and then took out his pipe and the three ten-kronor notes and showed them proudly. His loneliness made him confide in a stranger.

**What this does in the story.** The crofter's hospitality is the bait in the peddler's own theory that the world is a rattrap: the guest he entertains steals his thirty kronor the next morning. Yet the same hospitality, met again in Edla at the ironworks, is what finally frees the peddler from his own trap.

questions.question: Who was J. B. Kripalani? How did he help Gandhiji? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** J. B. Kripalani was **a lawyer and a Congress worker** who, in "Indigo", helps Gandhiji in the Champaran campaign. He was the one who met Gandhi at the station in Patna and took him to Rajendra Prasad's house, and he became one of the **lawyers who advised Gandhi on the peasants' case**.

**How he helped.** When Gandhi reached Motihari and was served with an order to leave the district, the lawyers of the district — Kripalani among them — offered to defend him, though they were nervous about defying the government. Gandhi told them he did not want them to go to jail for him unless they were ready; Kripalani and the others then stayed with the movement and helped in the courthouse, in the collection of the peasants' evidence and in the negotiations over the refund of the illegal rents.

**Kripalani's place in the movement.** The Champaran campaign was run on the strength of such volunteers, "the first lesson in the art of civil disobedience" for them as much as for the peasants.

questions.question: What is the difference between the thinking of Mr. Lamb and Derry? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The difference is between **acceptance and self-pity**. Mr. Lamb has one leg blown off in the war, wears a tin leg, and children call him "Lamey-Lamb" — yet he says, "I don't mind", and he keeps a garden, makes jelly from its apples and lets anyone come in. He believes that "it's all relative" and that what matters is not how you look but what you do with what you are given.

Derry, whose face was burnt by acid, has come to believe that everyone is afraid of him and that he has no right to a life among people. He hides in other people's gardens, expects to be stared at, and would rather be alone than be looked at. He thinks the world has been cruelly unfair to him.

**What changes.** Mr. Lamb makes him see that fear and ugliness are in the mind of the beholder, and by the end of the play Derry has decided to go back and to live.

questions.question: Who is Sophie? What things does she dream of becoming? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Sophie is a **young girl of a poor family** who has just left school; her friend Jansie and she are to work in the biscuit factory. She is a **dreamer** — Sophie is "very ambitious", and she lives in a world of fantasy that her practical friend cannot share.

**What she dreams of becoming.** She wants to be an **actress or a fashion designer**, and above all she wants to **own a boutique** of her own — "the most wonderful shop in the world", where she would be her own manager. She also dreams of the footballer **Danny Casey**, whom she claims to have met by the canal; she waits for his promised visit and builds a whole future on it.

**What the dream shows.** Jansie tells her the truth — that a boutique takes money she does not have — and Sophie's answer is to dream further. Her fantasies are her way of refusing the small, hard world her family lives in.

questions.question: What do the people of Roadside stand want from the city dwellers? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The people of the roadside stand want **the city dwellers' custom** — they want the passing cars to stop, look at their produce and buy it, so that they can "feel" some "city money" in hand.

**In the poem's words.** "Here far from the city we make our roadside stand / And ask for some city money to feel in hand / To try if it will not make our being expand, / And give us the life of the moving-pictures' promise." They sell wild berries, crook-necked squash and flowers, and with the money they would buy "the life of the moving-pictures' promise" — a little education, a doctor, a cinema.

**What they get instead.** The polished cars "halt" only to ask the way or to complain, and the poet's bitter conclusion is that the poor are left to wait, while the "greedy good-doers" arrive to reorganise them.

questions.question: What are the things of beauty that help us during dark times? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Keats lists the **beauties of nature** — the sun, the moon, the old and young trees that give shade, the daffodils, the clear rills that make a "cooling covert against the hot season", the "mid forest brake" rich with musk-rose blooms, and the "grandeur of the dooms" of the mighty dead.

**How they help.** Each of these " pours some shape of beauty" which "moves away the pall / From our dark spirits". A thing of beauty keeps "a bower quiet for us", gives us sleep "full of sweet dreams, and health, and quiet breathing", and binds us to the earth with "a flowery band" that ties us to life even when it is "gloomy".

**In one line.** The lovely things of the world are the medicine of the sad mind: their beauty never fades, and its influence increases with time.

questions.question: Who was Roger Skunk? What was his main problem? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Roger Skunk is a **small animal — a young skunk** — in Jack's bedtime story in "Should Wizard Hit Mommy?". He is so small that he has little to do with the world of the grown-ups, and he lives with his mother.

**His main problem** is that **he smells very bad**. His bad smell keeps all the other little creatures away: "no one played with him". He is left alone and weeps over his fate. So he goes to the wise old owl, who sends him to the wizard; the wizard takes seven pennies and gives him the smell of a rose, and Roger is at last able to play with the other animals.

**What follows.** His mother is angry — "he is a skunk and he must smell like a skunk" — and takes him back to the wizard to be changed again; Jo, who is being told the story, wants the mother punished, and her father refuses to change the ending.

questions.question: How did Derry's life change after meeting Mr. Lamb? (Answer in maximum 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Before meeting Mr. Lamb, Derry had **withdrawn from everyone**: he believed that people were afraid of his burnt face, he avoided being looked at, and he had decided that he "wouldn't go anywhere" and would live alone.

**What changed.** Mr. Lamb greeted him without pity, told him that "it's all relative" and that "you could do anything, be anything", and showed him that a man with a tin leg could still keep a garden, make jelly and be happy. Derry's mother had warned him to stay away from the old man, but he came back — and by the end of the play he says, "I'm going to be all right", and weeps with relief.

**The cost of the change.** He finds Mr. Lamb dead at the foot of the ladder, so the play leaves him with both a loss and a gift: the one person who understood him is gone, and his confidence has to be carried forward without him.

questions.question: You are Sports Secretary of Lalwani Public School, Udaipur. Draft a notice for the school board asking the students to give their names for participation in various events to be held on the annual sports day of your school. You are Lalit/Lalita. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**LALWANI PUBLIC SCHOOL, UDAIPUR**

**NOTICE**

*15 November 2024*

**ANNUAL SPORTS DAY — ENTRIES INVITED**

The annual sports day of the school will be held on **Saturday, 7 December 2024, from 8 a.m. on the school ground**. Students who wish to take part in any of the following events should give their names to the undersigned **on or before 25 November 2024**, through their class teacher:

1. **Track events** — 100 m, 200 m, 400 m, relay (4 × 100 m), 1500 m
2. **Field events** — long jump, high jump, shot put, javelin
3. **Team games** — kho-kho, volleyball, kabaddi, basketball (inter-house)
4. **Special events** — three-legged race, sack race, tug of war, and a 100 m race for teachers

Every participant must bring a **medical fitness certificate** signed by a parent or a doctor, and must report to the ground half an hour before the event. Participants are expected to wear the house vest and white shorts. The names of the selected students and the final schedule will be put up on the notice board on 30 November.

**Lalita**
Sports Secretary

**Format points.** The name of the institution, the word NOTICE, the date, the event with **date and venue**, the full list of events, the **deadline and manner of entry**, the conditions (fitness certificate, dress, reporting time) and the signature with the designation. A 250-word limit allows the list of events to be complete — do not shorten it to one line.

questions.question: The crisis caused by the COVID-19 virus has forced us to think about the upliftment of health facilities in our state. Write a letter as Sunita/Sameer of 223/D, Main Road, Ranchi, to the Editor of a national daily, discussing the health facilities of our city and the improvements needed. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**223/D, Main Road**
**Ranchi**
**18 August 2024**

The Editor
*The Times of India*
New Delhi

**Subject: The state of health facilities in Ranchi and the improvements needed**

Sir

Through the columns of your esteemed national daily I wish to draw the attention of the government to the condition of the health facilities in our city, which the COVID-19 crisis has exposed.

During the pandemic the RIMS and the district hospital ran out of oxygen, ventilators and isolation beds within days. Patients were turned away from one hospital to another, and families queued outside oxygen plants with empty cylinders. The smaller primary health centres in the blocks have no doctor after 2 p.m., no ambulance and no stock of basic medicines. Private testing was priced out of the reach of the ordinary family.

The improvements needed are clear. First, the **oxygen supply and the number of critical-care beds** must be increased in every district hospital — this is a recurring cost that cannot be postponed again. Second, **primary health centres must be staffed and stocked** and connected by a working ambulance service. Third, **testing and vaccination must be free and evenly spread** in the villages. Fourth, the government must audit private hospitals that overcharge patients during an epidemic.

A health system built in a crisis should not be allowed to decay when the crisis passes. I hope your paper will press the matter with the authorities.

Yours faithfully
**Sunita**

**Format points.** Address and date, addressee, a clear subject line, the **specific problems** with instances, a numbered list of improvements, and a formal close — all within 250 words.

questions.question: You are Manav/Manavi of DPS Bokaro. Recently a yoga and meditation programme was organised in your school to enhance the mental health of the students. Write a report on it. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**YOGA AND MEDITATION PROGRAMME HELD AT DPS BOKARO**

*By Manavi, Class XII*

**Bokaro, 10 September 2024.** A two-day **yoga and meditation programme** was organised in our school on 8 and 9 September to enhance the mental health of the students, especially in the weeks before the board examinations.

The programme was conducted by **Sri Anand Sharma of the Patanjali Yogpeeth**, assisted by two physical education teachers of the school. The first day began at 6.30 a.m. with a demonstration of *asanas* — *tadasana*, *vrikshasana*, *bhujangasana* and *shavasana* — which the students then practised on mats laid out on the school ground. The instructor explained the importance of correct breathing and posture and warned against practising on a full stomach.

The second day was devoted to **meditation and stress management**. The students were taught a simple twenty-minute breathing exercise to be done before study, and a short question-answer session followed: boys and girls asked about sleeplessness, examination anxiety and the use of mobile phones at night. About six hundred students of classes IX to XII took part.

The Principal thanked the instructors and announced that **a fifteen-minute yoga session would begin every school day** from the next week.

**Format points.** Headline, byline, date and place, **who organised it, who conducted it, what was done on each day, how many attended**, and what will follow — all in the past tense and third person, within 250 words.

questions.question: You have received training in First Aid, as a member of Red Cross Society, arranged by your school. Prepare a report to be published in your school magazine about your training. Sign as Sagar/Sagarika. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**FIRST AID TRAINING FOR RED CROSS VOLUNTEERS**

*By Sagarika, Class XII*

**Bokaro, 22 July 2024.** A three-day **First Aid training camp** was arranged by our school for the members of its Red Cross Society, from 18 to 20 July, in the school auditorium.

The training was given by **Dr. R. N. Prasad of the Bokaro General Hospital** and two trained nurses. On the first day we were taught how to **examine an injured person safely** — checking breathing, pulse and bleeding without moving a suspected fracture — and how to put a patient in the recovery position. The second day was given to **practical bandaging**: the triangular bandage for the head and the arm, the splint for a broken limb, and the treatment of burns, cuts and snake-bite. On the third day we practised **cardiopulmonary resuscitation on a dummy** and learned how to shift a patient on a stretcher and how to inform the family and the ambulance service.

On the last afternoon each volunteer was examined in a mock accident drill, and all forty-two of us received a certificate. The Principal said the volunteers would now assist at school functions and sports meets.

**What the training taught us.** In an emergency the first five minutes matter more than the hospital, and the first duty of a bystander is not to panic.

**Format points.** Headline, byline, dates and place, a day-by-day account of the training, the numbers and the certificate, and a concluding reflection — within 250 words.

questions.question: Every teenager has a dream to achieve something in life. What they are going to become tomorrow depends on what our youth dream today. Write an article on what 'I want to be in life'. You are Simranjit/Smita. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**WHAT I WANT TO BE IN LIFE**

*— Smita*

Every teenager has a dream to achieve something in life, and what we are going to become tomorrow depends on what our youth dream today. I want to be a **doctor** — not for the white coat or the respect it carries, but because of a night I have never forgotten.

When I was twelve my grandmother fell ill in our village. There was no doctor within twenty kilometres, and the nearest hospital could be reached only by a jeep that arrived four hours later. She survived, but the waiting taught me something that no lesson in school could: that in our country the distance to a doctor is still, for millions of people, the distance between life and death.

I know what this dream asks of me. It means two more years of biology, then the entrance examination, then five years of medical college and a lifetime of study after that. It will mean nights without sleep and days without rest. I have begun already: I read about the human body, I volunteer at the health camp that our school holds every winter, and I have learnt the first elements of first aid.

But I do not want to be only a doctor in a city. I want to be the doctor who returns to a village like mine, where the jeep takes four hours.

**Format points.** A title with the writer's name, a personal reason rather than a general one, an honest account of **what the ambition requires**, and a concrete resolution — within 250 words.

questions.question: You are the Youth Secretary of your school. Your school is organising a blood donation camp for a noble cause. Write a letter to your friend describing this as a social work for mankind. (Answer in maximum 250 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**12, Sector IV**
**Bokaro**
**18 September 2024**

My dear Aditya

I have been wanting to write to you for weeks, and today I have something worth writing about. Our school is organising a **blood donation camp** on 2 October as part of the Gandhi Jayanti programme, and as Youth Secretary I have been running about the corridors with posters and permission letters.

I want to tell you what this camp means to me. The district blood bank told us that it runs short of blood almost every fortnight: the supply comes from the town hospital, and the villages around us have nothing. A single donation of 350 ml can be used for up to three patients, and the body replaces it within weeks. When we asked who would receive it, the doctor smiled and said, "A woman in childbirth, a boy hurt in an accident, a child with thalassaemia. You will never meet them."

That sentence has stayed with me. We think of social work as something large — a movement, a rally, a campaign — but here is a thing a sixteen-year-old can do in twenty minutes, with a little pain and a great deal of good, and it will be someone's life. Thirty-two students and six teachers have already signed up.

Do write back and tell me what your school is doing this Gandhi Jayanti. Give my regards to uncle and aunt.

Your loving friend
**Sagarika**

**Format points.** An informal letter gives the sender's address and date, a familiar salutation and closing, personal feeling and **one concrete piece of information**, all in a conversational tone — within 250 words.
